sections.title: 🎯 What You'll Learn
sections.content:
Let’s explore how to use Java’s built-in math tools to make calculations easier! No need to reinvent the wheel—Java’s `Math` class has you covered.

• How to use `Math.pow()` for exponents (like 2³)
• Why the `Math` class is your math buddy
• Common math operations you’ll use daily

sections.title: 💡 Concept Explanation
sections.content:
Imagine you’re baking a cake. Instead of measuring ingredients from scratch, you use pre-measured cups—saves time, right? The `Math` class is like those pre-measured cups for programming!

Java’s `Math` class gives you ready-to-use methods for common calculations. No need to write complex logic for exponents, square roots, or rounding—just call a method!

• **Exponents**: `Math.pow(a, b)` calculates `a` raised to the power of `b` (e.g., `2³ = 8`)
• **Precision**: Works with `double` values (e.g., `Math.pow(4, 0.5) = 2.0`)
• **Easy to use**: Just write `Math.pow(base, exponent)`—no extra setup needed!

steps.title: Call the Method
steps.description: You tell Java what numbers to use. For example, `Math.pow(2, 3)` means "2 raised to the power of 3."

steps.title: Calculation Happens
steps.description: Java does the math behind the scenes: `2 * 2 * 2 = 8`.

steps.title: Return the Result
steps.description: The method gives back the answer as a `double`. Here, it returns `8.0`.

sections.title: ⚡ Key Points
points: ✓ `Math.pow(a, b)` = `a` raised to the power of `b` (e.g., `Math.pow(3, 2) = 9.0`)
✓ Always returns a `double` (even if the result is a whole number like `8.0`)
✓ Works with decimals (e.g., `Math.pow(4, 0.5) = 2.0` for square roots)
✓ No need to import—`Math` is built into Java!
✓ Use it for exponents, roots, and more—no manual loops needed!

sections.title: 🔥 Tips & Mistakes
dos: Use `Math.pow()` for exponents—it’s cleaner than loops
Remember the result is a `double` (e.g., `8.0` instead of `8`)
donts: Don’t forget the `Math.` prefix (e.g., `pow(2, 3)` won’t work alone)
Avoid using it for simple multiplication (e.g., `Math.pow(2, 2)` is overkill for `2 * 2`)
Don’t mix up the order—`Math.pow(3, 2)` is `9`, not `6`!
sections.protip: For square roots, use `Math.sqrt()` instead of `Math.pow(x, 0.5)`—it’s clearer and faster!

sections.title: 🌍 Real World Use
sections.content: Where is `Math.pow()` used in real apps?

examples.how: Computes distances, physics (e.g., projectile motion), or scaling effects
Handles exponents, roots, and logarithmic functions

problem.description:
Write a program that calculates the area of a circle using the formula `π * r²`. Use `Math.pow()` to compute `r²` (radius squared).

Example: If the radius is `5`, the area should be `78.53981633974483`.
hints: Use `Math.PI` for π (no need to define it yourself!)
problem.explanation: We used `Math.pow(radius, 2)` to square the radius and `Math.PI` for π. The formula `π * r²` is now clean and easy to read!

sections.title: 📝 Summary
points: 📌 `Math.pow(a, b)` is your go-to for exponents—no loops needed!
📌 Practice with real-world formulas (like circle area or compound interest)
📌 Ready for the next topic: `Math.sqrt()` and rounding methods!
